title: Controlling Public Module APIs knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which mental model best explains “Controlling Public Module APIs” in Dart Sass?
options: The browser executes Sass source directly, so a compilation step is unnecessary.
Readable SCSS guarantees correct browser rendering, accessibility, and performance without output review.
The best solution is always to replace native CSS behavior with a new Sass abstraction.

The Sass module system separates member definitions from their use: `@use` provides namespaced access and loads a module once, while `@forward` exposes selected members through a library entrypoint. This makes dependency direction and public APIs easier to review.
questions.answer_key: The Sass module system separates member definitions from their use: `@use` provides namespaced access and loads a module once, while `@forward` exposes selected members through a library entrypoint. This makes dependency direction and public APIs easier to review.
questions.explanation: The Sass module system separates member definitions from their use: `@use` provides namespaced access and loads a module once, while `@forward` exposes selected members through a library entrypoint. This makes dependency direction and public APIs easier to review. The alternative choices confuse Sass compilation with browser execution or claim guarantees that require independent tests.

questions.prompt: When applying “Forwarding selected members”, which approach is the most reliable?
options: Prefer deeply nested selectors because fewer source lines always mean simpler and safer CSS.
Silence every warning before determining whether it identifies a deprecated or incorrect construct.
For forwarding selected members, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.
Skip compilation and infer the final selector list and property values from the source file alone.
questions.answer_key: For forwarding selected members, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.
questions.explanation: For forwarding selected members, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation. Compare the compiled output with the stated intent and preserve browser-native behavior where it is required.

questions.prompt: Which review decision most directly supports maintainability for “Controlling Public Module APIs”?
options: Expose internal implementation details as public API and postpone documentation until after release.

For new work, prefer Dart Sass and the module system. Keep legacy patterns only when maintaining an older codebase, migrate in small batches, and compare compiled CSS because a successful compile does not alone guarantee equivalent output.
Generate every possible selector or theme combination, even when most variants are never used.
Treat successful compilation as proof that the interface is accessible and behaves correctly in every browser.
questions.answer_key: For new work, prefer Dart Sass and the module system. Keep legacy patterns only when maintaining an older codebase, migrate in small batches, and compare compiled CSS because a successful compile does not alone guarantee equivalent output.
questions.explanation: For new work, prefer Dart Sass and the module system. Keep legacy patterns only when maintaining an older codebase, migrate in small batches, and compare compiled CSS because a successful compile does not alone guarantee equivalent output. The other choices increase output, assume unverified behavior, or make the public interface harder to maintain.
